2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: High concern: Across 135 countries and a nominal 1990-2015 study window (3,510 potential country-years), effective sample sizes drop to N = 1,713, 1,593, and 1,087 in global models (Tables 2-4, PDF pp. 11-13) and to N = 351, 408, and 262 (1,021 total; ~71% missing relative to 1990-2015) in income-group models (Tables 5-7, PDF pp. 14-17) due to shorter WGI/ODA windows and missing female education observations, with no missing-data diagnostics, listwise-deletion assessment, or sensitivity checks reported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern: Although country and year fixed effects, World Bank income-group stratification, and 1-period lags on female primary completion and ODA are used (Sections 2.2 and 2.4, PDF pp. 5-9), severe residual confounding remains: global regressions (Tables 2-4) enter LogGNI, Female, and Agriculture one at a time in separate equations due to multicollinearity (reintroducing omitted-variable bias), subgroup models (Tables 5-7) drop governance covariates via preliminary Wald tests, 1-year lags do not resolve simultaneity, and major time-varying confounders (domestic public WASH spending, urbanization, conflict, climatic shocks) are unmeasured.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Weak (High concern): Legal and institutional governance is operationalized solely through national perception-based World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (Rule of Law, Regulatory Quality, Control of Corruption, Government Effectiveness, Voice and Accountability, Political Stability) rather than de jure water statutes, rural service regulations, or subnational enforcement measures; critically, these continuous (-2.5 to +2.5) scores are collapsed into three dummy categories ('Very weak', 'Weak', 'Good') in Figure 2 (PDF p. 10) with all numerical threshold cutoffs omitted from both Figure 2 and the text.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern: While economic and water variables come from standard World Bank, UNESCO, OECD, and WHO/UNICEF JMP databases, the six governance exposures are discretized into dummy categories whose numerical cutoffs are omitted from Figure 2 (PDF p. 10), WGI temporal variation may reflect changing data sources rather than actual governance shifts (PDF p. 10), female primary completion rate is an unadjusted gross intake proxy that ignores final-year dropouts and can exceed 100% (PDF p. 8), and aggregate JMP access percentages do not capture supply regularity or water quality (PDF p. 2).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate (Some concern): Outcomes use standardized WHO/UNICEF JMP definitions for rural drinking-water coverage disaggregated into total improved, piped on premises, and other improved sources (Section 2.3, PDF p. 6), improving upon undifferentiated 'improved' metrics; however, outcome summary statistics by stratum are omitted from Table 1, exact JMP vintage and cross-year survey interpolation procedures are not detailed, and nominal facility access does not measure continuity or potability (PDF p. 2).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern: No pre-analysis plan or protocol registration exists; in income-stratum regressions (Tables 5-7, PDF pp. 14-17), governance indicators are selectively included or excluded based on preliminary Wald tests (Tables A4-A6, PDF pp. 19-20), creating data-driven specification selection; Section 3.2 (PDF p. 15) claims rural population growth significantly increases piped water access in middle-high-income countries whereas the reported Table 5 coefficient (0.267, SE 0.236) is statistically non-significant; Tables A4-A6 mislabel Wald p-values as standard errors; and Tables 6-7 contain misaligned rows for regulatory quality variables.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Some to High concern: Country eligibility is defined by objective World Bank 2015 GNI per capita thresholds (Tables A1-A3, PDF pp. 18-19; noting a minor discrepancy between 51 lower-middle-income countries stated on PDF p. 4 and 50 listed in Table A2), but classifying countries across 1990-2015 using end-of-period 2015 income groups conditions subgroup stratification on post-baseline economic performance, and heavy unaddressed country-year missingness selects toward countries and years with complete statistical reporting.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the criteria for inclusion in the sample clearly defined?
domain_ratings.justification: Country-level eligibility criteria are clearly defined using World Bank (2015) FY2016 Atlas GNI per capita thresholds (<$1,045 low-income; $1,045-$4,125 lower-middle-income; $4,125-$12,736 upper-middle-income, excluding high-income >=$12,736), with included countries listed in Appendix Tables A1-A3. Note minor inconsistencies: text states 51 lower-middle-income countries while Table A2 lists 50 (including 'Bolovia'), and exclusion rules for missing country-years are not stated.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.1 (PDF p. 4); Appendix A, Tables A1-A3 (PDF pp. 18-19)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail?
domain_ratings.justification: Although included countries are listed by income tier (Tables A1-A3) and explanatory variable means and standard deviations are reported by group (Table 1), key panel setting details are missing: Table 1 omits descriptive statistics for all three rural water access outcomes, the exact years available for WGI indicators are unstated, and the composition of the heavily unbalanced regression samples (e.g., N = 262, 408, and 351 in Tables 5-7 out of >3,000 nominal country-years over 1990-2015) is not described.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 1 (PDF p. 3); Section 2.1 (PDF p. 4); Section 2.4, Table 1 (PDF p. 7); Tables 2-7 (PDF pp. 11-17); Tables A1-A3 (PDF pp. 18-19)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Macroeconomic and demographic indicators come from standard international databases (World Bank, UNESCO, OECD QWIDS), but all six Worldwide Governance Indicators are transformed into three categorical dummy variables ('Very weak', 'Weak', 'Good') using a custom scale in Figure 2 that omits every numerical cutoff value from both the figure and the text, preventing verification or replication. Furthermore, the authors note that WGI changes over time may reflect changes in data sources rather than governance (PDF p. 10) and that female primary completion rate lacks dropout adjustment and can exceed 100% (PDF p. 8).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were objective, standard criteria used for measurement of the condition?
domain_ratings.justification: Standardized international classifications are applied across all countries: World Bank Atlas GNI per capita thresholds define developing-country income strata (Section 2.1) and WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) criteria define rural drinking-water source categories (Section 2.3), although country income strata are fixed at 2015 levels across the entire 1990-2015 panel.

The authors explicitly identify country-specific unobserved heterogeneity, common year shocks, national income (GNI), female education, agricultural GDP share, rural population growth, water/sanitation ODA, six governance dimensions, and potential simultaneity/endogeneity between water access and both female primary completion rate and foreign aid.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: Strategies to address confounding are explicitly stated: country and year fixed effects (Equation 1), stratification into three World Bank income tiers, and one-period lags on female primary completion rate and ODA to mitigate reverse causality (though their implementation in global models reintroduces omitted-variable bias by entering collinear core variables separately).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Outcomes are measured using standardized WHO/UNICEF JMP rural drinking-water definitions disaggregated into total improved, piped on premises, and other improved sources, addressing a major limitation of aggregated 'improved' indicators; inherent limitations (inability to capture continuity of supply or water quality, and reliance on interpolated national survey series) are acknowledged on PDF p. 2.

While two-way fixed effects estimated via Prais-Winsten GLS ('xtpcse') account for panel heteroskedasticity and AR(1) serial correlation, major analytical and reporting flaws undermine validity: (1) to avoid multicollinearity in global models (Tables 2-4), LogGNI, Female, and Agriculture are estimated in separate regressions omitting the other two major confounders, inducing omitted-variable bias; (2) governance variables in subgroup models (Tables 5-7) are selectively dropped via preliminary Wald tests (Tables A4-A6), invalidating post-selection inference; (3) income stratification over 1990-2015 conditions on endline 2015 GNI; (4) Section 2.2 inaccurately asserts Hausman tests cannot be implemented under heteroskedasticity/autocorrelation; and (5) Section 3.2 (PDF p. 15) claims rural population growth significantly increases piped water in middle-high-income countries when Table 5 shows 0.267 (SE 0.236, non-significant), Tables A4-A6 mislabel p-values as standard errors, and Tables 6-7 misalign regulatory dummy rows.
domain_ratings.where_found: Section 2.2 (PDF pp. 5-6); Section 3.1-3.4, Tables 2-7 (PDF pp. 10-17); Appendix A, Tables A4-A6 (PDF pp. 19-20)

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Gomez, Perdiguero, and Sanz (2019) conduct an observational macro-panel regression analyzing national socioeconomic and governance correlates of rural drinking-water coverage (total improved, piped on premises, and other improved sources) across 135 low- and middle-income countries over a nominal 1990-2015 period using two-way (country and year) fixed-effects Prais-Winsten GLS models with heteroskedastic and panel-specific AR(1) errors. Methodological strengths include disaggregating WHO/UNICEF JMP rural water coverage into piped on premises versus other improved sources, stratifying analyses by World Bank income tiers, and accounting for time-invariant country heterogeneity, common year shocks, and serial correlation. However, overall methodological concern is High (Q1, Q4, Q5, Q6, Q7 = Yes; Q2, Q3 = Unclear; Q8 = No). First, all six Worldwide Governance Indicators (including Rule of Law and Regulatory Quality) are collapsed into three dummy categories ('Very weak', 'Weak', 'Good') in Figure 2, but all numerical cutoff values are omitted from Figure 2 and the text, rendering the primary institutional exposures unverifiable. Second, unaddressed missing data reduces the effective sample from 3,510 potential country-years (135 countries x 26 years) to N = 1,087-1,713 in global models and N = 1,021 total across the three income-group models (~71% missingness), with no missing-data diagnostics or outcome summary statistics reported. Third, global regressions enter LogGNI, female primary completion, and agriculture into separate equations due to multicollinearity (inducing severe omitted-variable bias), while subgroup regressions selectively drop governance variables via preliminary Wald tests and stratify 1990-2015 trajectories on end-of-period (2015) GNI per capita. Finally, several reporting errors appear (claiming statistical significance on p. 15 for an insignificant Table 5 piped-water rural growth coefficient of 0.267 [SE 0.236], mislabeling Wald p-values as standard errors in Tables A4-A6, and misaligning rows in Tables 6-7).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Cross-national longitudinal macro-panel observational regression (two-way country and year fixed-effects Prais-Winsten GLS panel analysis of 135 low- and middle-income countries, nominally 1990-2015) without a discrete policy/intervention comparator
raw_response.where_found_summary: Section 1 Introduction (PDF pp. 2-4); Section 2 Materials and Methods, Sections 2.1-2.4, Table 1, and Figure 2 (PDF pp. 4-10); Section 3 Results, Sections 3.1-3.4, and Tables 2-7 (PDF pp. 10-17); Appendix A, Tables A1-A6 (PDF pp. 18-20).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: Under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §1, the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies covers quantitative cross-sectional surveys and observational regressions without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Although the dataset has a country-year panel structure (nominally 1990-2015), the study evaluates general macroeconomic and governance correlates rather than a discrete policy or intervention with treatment/control arms (ruling out ROBINS-I) and models aggregate ecological prevalence of rural water coverage rather than following exposed and unexposed cohorts initially free of an incident outcome (ruling out JBI Cohort Studies).
